historyReviewBoundary: All 115 histories have author source checks. Final independent review covered metadata and numerical checks for all 115 classes, 12 deeper class targets and source-gap samples in seven classes. It did not independently verify every passage of every cited source.

history.name: Anilide non-opioid analgesics

starting.description: The reported antipyretic effect of synthetic acetanilide became an observed lead for research on related antipyretics, including phenacetin and the subsequent paracetamol search. A later, distinct observation that paracetamol was a prominent acetanilide metabolite in plasma prompted appraisal of its analgesic activity.

inspiration.description: An observed antipyretic effect of synthetic acetanilide, clinical response including a reported case of pain relief, and the later acetanilide-to-paracetamol metabolic relationship pertain to distinct stages; the metabolite is not described as an endogenous starting template.

steps.description: Cahn and Hepp reported antipyretic effects of acetanilide; a contemporary review describes fortunate access and subsequent tests in animals and fever patients, including a report of pain relief in one rheumatism case.

Acetanilide's success and adverse effects prompted research on related chemicals; phenacetin was prepared and tested as another antipyretic. Accounts disagree about the precise role of luck and who initiated the chemistry.

Paracetamol, described retrospectively as chemically synthesized by Morse in 1878, was assessed during the later search for alternatives to phenacetin. Von Mering reported clinical work in 1893; accounts differ about the first trial date.

Brodie and Axelrod's 1948 investigation of acetanilide metabolism found substantial N-acetyl-p-aminophenol; its high plasma concentration prompted analgesic appraisal. Flinn and Brodie's 1948 heat-radiation study reported analgesic activity.

The later metabolic findings contributed to renewed interest and market introduction of paracetamol in the 1950s; this was a later development, not its original synthesis or first clinical assessment.

design.description: Chemists prepared and pharmacologists tested related structures in pursuit of effective antipyresis with fewer adverse effects; phenacetin and paracetamol are structurally distinct compounds. The review reports that paracetamol itself had been prepared before the therapeutic search. This was a change in active chemical structure and biological testing, not merely a delivery adjustment.

circumstances.description: The early acquisition of the antipyretic preparation was described as fortunate. The subsequent search among related chemicals and the later metabolite investigation and pain-threshold appraisal were deliberate; this does not assert that every observation in the overall sequence was planned or accidental.

limits: The cohort is paracetamol alone; acetanilide and phenacetin are historically relevant leads, not additional cohort biographies.
S1 supports the reported acetanilide effect and clinical testing, but not the detailed pharmacy anecdote. S2, S4, S5 and S6 are retrospective accounts and may share source ancestry.

The 1948 acetanilide-to-paracetamol metabolism and analgesic work is a later development/rediscovery contribution, not the chemical invention of paracetamol or its first clinical trial. The separate 1949 phenacetin metabolism report was located but not read.
The class boundary does not assert that paracetamol is a conventional peripheral NSAID, nor does this record settle its modern mechanism or prove a universal comparative safety ranking.
conflicts: S2 and S5 repeat the naphthalene/worms/pharmacy story; S4 explicitly says it cannot be substantiated. S1's near-contemporary review describes a fortunate occurrence but does not establish the detailed anecdote.

S2 reports competing accounts of whether luck or systematic chemistry was central to phenacetin's discovery; S4 describes an acetanilide-led commercial and chemical project. These differences do not negate the preceding observed acetanilide effect.

S6 dates the first reported clinical use to 1887 while citing the 1893 von Mering paper; S5 describes a trial in 1893. Without reading the primary report, a study-versus-publication distinction is possible but the earliest-use date remains unresolved.

S5's attribution of 1940s findings to phenacetin should not be transferred to S3: S3 directly studied acetanilide, while the separate phenacetin report is from 1949. S3's claim about how much analgesia was mediated by the metabolite is reported as its authors' historical conclusion, not independently established here.
gaps: The 1886 Cahn-Hepp original and von Mering's 1893 original were located but HathiTrust returned HTTP 403; the detailed original circumstances, exact first clinical-use date and original adverse-effect findings remain unverified.
The 1878 Morse original was identified from publisher metadata but not read; S6 is the cited retrospective source for its link to paracetamol, not proof of Morse's purpose.

Flinn and Brodie's 1948 pain-threshold article was read only as the indexed publisher abstract; the separate 1949 Brodie-Axelrod phenacetin report was not read. A proposed impurity as the explanation for von Mering's adverse-effect observation remains hypothetical.

humanContributionInterpretation.summary: Antipyretic benefit and adverse effects of preceding drugs helped motivate safer related analgesics.
